meta.titre: Sentence Structure: clauses, correct sentences, parallelism and -ing forms

source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L English Language past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: A Lower Sixth student writes in an essay, "Walking to school, the rain started." Read literally, the rain was walking to school. Slips like this are not carelessness about vocabulary: they come from a weak grasp of how a sentence is built. At A Level, grammar items ask you to pick the correctly written sentence, to complete a structure so that its parts match, and to say what job a word does in a sentence. This course gives you the building blocks, the faults examiners expect you to spot, and a method to find the one correct option.

items: A sentence has a subject and a verb and expresses a complete thought.
Conjunctions such as and, but, because and although join words, phrases and clauses.
Nouns name things, verbs show actions or states, adjectives describe nouns and adverbs describe verbs.

sections.titre: Sentence structure: clauses, types of sentence and common faults
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Building blocks
A **clause** has its own subject and finite verb. A **main (independent) clause** makes sense alone; a **subordinate clause** depends on a main clause. A **phrase** is a group of words without its own subject and finite verb ("after the rain", "to win the match").

### Four sentence types
| Type | Structure | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Simple | one main clause | The rain stopped. |
| Compound | main clauses joined by and, but, or, so, yet, or a semicolon | The rain stopped, and the match resumed. |
| Complex | a main clause and a subordinate clause | When the rain stopped, the match resumed. |
| Compound-complex | two main clauses and a subordinate clause | When the rain stopped, the match resumed, but many spectators had already left. |

### Faults to spot and repair
| Fault | Faulty sentence | Repair |
|---|---|---|
| Fragment | Because the road was flooded. | Because the road was flooded, we stayed at home. |
| Comma splice | The road was flooded, we stayed at home. | The road was flooded, so we stayed at home. |
| Dangling modifier | Walking home, the rain soaked my shirt. | Walking home, I was soaked by the rain. |
| Agreement | Each of the pupils have a book. | Each of the pupils has a book. |
| Faulty parallelism | She likes swimming, to run and playing football. | She likes swimming, running and playing football. |

An opening participle phrase must describe the **subject** of the main clause. After **each, every, either, neither** the verb is singular. With **neither ... nor** the verb agrees with the nearer subject: "Neither the teacher nor the pupils were present." Items joined by and, or and but must have the same grammatical form, for example by working hard and by listening carefully.

### -ing forms and verb patterns
A **gerund** is a verbal noun: it acts as subject, object or the word after a preposition ("Swimming is good exercise"; "She is tired of waiting"). A quick test is to replace it with "it". A **present participle** forms continuous tenses ("is waiting") or describes a noun or the subject ("the barking dog"; "Hearing the news, she wept"). After a preposition use the gerund: interested in learning, by working. Verbs such as enjoy, avoid, finish, suggest, mind and admit take a gerund; decide, hope, refuse, promise, manage and agree take an infinitive.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When an item lists four sentences and asks for the one without error.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Test each option for the same checklist: a complete main clause, no comma splice, correct agreement, a participle phrase that matches the subject, parallel items, and the right verb pattern (gerund or infinitive). Cross out the options with a fault. Only one option should survive; read it again to be sure.

variantes.nom: What is the function of the underlined word?
variantes.quand_utiliser: When you must classify a word (noun, gerund, participle, adjective, adverb) in a sentence.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Look at what the word does, not at how it is spelt. A word ending in -ing after a preposition ("tired of writing") is a gerund, a noun in function. In "is writing" it is part of the verb. In "the crying baby" it describes the noun (a participle used as an adjective). Replace the word with "it" to test for a noun function.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a sentence has a gap after and, or or but, or after a phrase such as not only.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Copy the form of the element before the conjunction. If the first item is by + -ing, the second must also be a gerund phrase: "by working hard and by listening carefully" or "by working hard and listening carefully". Reject an option that changes the form, such as a noun or an infinitive.

sections.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following sentences is correctly written?

A. Having finished the exam early, the invigilator allowed Tabe to leave.
B. The road was blocked, nobody could pass.
C. Neither the driver nor the passengers were hurt in the accident.
D. She enjoys to swim and playing football.

etapes.justification: An opening participle phrase must describe the subject of the main clause.
etapes.resultat_markdown: "Having finished the exam early" would describe the invigilator, who did not take the exam. This is a dangling modifier. A is wrong.

etapes.justification: Two main clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone.
etapes.resultat_markdown: "The road was blocked" and "nobody could pass" are main clauses joined by a comma. This is a comma splice. B is wrong.

etapes.justification: Enjoy takes a gerund, and the items after and must be parallel.
etapes.resultat_markdown: "Enjoys to swim" uses an infinitive after enjoy, and "to swim" is not parallel with "playing". D is wrong.

etapes.justification: With neither ... nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The nearer subject is "passengers", which is plural, so "were" is correct. The sentence has a complete main clause and no other fault.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The correct sentence is **C**. A has a dangling modifier, B a comma splice and D a wrong verb pattern with faulty parallelism.

items.erreur_markdown: "Because the match was cancelled." (written as a full sentence)
items.pourquoi_faux: It is a subordinate clause only. Because leaves the thought incomplete.
items.correction_markdown: "Because the match was cancelled, the players went home."

items.erreur_markdown: "The manager is strict, he punishes lateness."
items.pourquoi_faux: Two main clauses are joined by a comma only (comma splice).
items.correction_markdown: "The manager is strict, and he punishes lateness." or "The manager is strict; he punishes lateness."

items.erreur_markdown: "Each of the pupils have a textbook."
items.pourquoi_faux: The subject of the sentence is each, which is singular. The plural word pupils is not the subject.

items.erreur_markdown: "Running down the hill, the hat fell off."
items.pourquoi_faux: The participle phrase should describe the subject, but the hat did not run.
items.correction_markdown: "Running down the hill, Ada lost her hat."

items.pourquoi_faux: Enjoy is followed by a gerund, not an infinitive.

items.enonce_markdown:
Say whether each sentence is simple, compound, complex or compound-complex.

(a) The bell rang.
(b) The bell rang, and the pupils ran out.
(c) Although it was late, the market was still busy.
(d) The traders who sell fish arrive early, but the farmers come later.
items.solution_markdown: **(a) simple**: one main clause. **(b) compound**: two main clauses joined by and. **(c) complex**: one main clause with a subordinate clause beginning with although. **(d) compound-complex**: two main clauses joined by but, and a subordinate (relative) clause "who sell fish".

items.enonce_markdown:
Rewrite each faulty sentence correctly.

(a) Although she studied hard.
(b) The generator broke down, the lesson continued by candlelight.
(c) Our teacher advised us to revise daily, sleeping early and to avoid worry.
items.solution_markdown: **(a)** Add a main clause: "Although she studied hard, she was still nervous." **(b)** Join the clauses correctly: "The generator broke down, but the lesson continued by candlelight." (or use a semicolon or a full stop). **(c)** Make the items parallel: "Our teacher advised us to revise daily, to sleep early and to avoid worry."

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) State the function of the word in bold: gerund, present participle in a verb, or participle used as an adjective.
   (i) **Dancing** is her favourite hobby.
   (ii) The crowd is **dancing** in the street.
   (iii) The **barking** dog woke the whole street.
   (iv) He earned money by **selling** mangoes.
(b) Rewrite correctly: "Waiting for the bus, the rain soaked my clothes."
items.solution_markdown:
**(a)(i) gerund**, subject of the sentence. **(ii) present participle** in the continuous verb "is dancing". **(iii) participle used as an adjective**, describing "dog". **(iv) gerund**, the word after the preposition "by".
**(b)** The participle phrase does not describe the rain, so a new subject is needed: "Waiting for the bus, I was soaked by the rain." or "While I was waiting for the bus, the rain soaked my clothes."

items_markdown: A clause has its own subject and finite verb; learn the four sentence types: simple, compound, complex, compound-complex.
Check every option for fragments, comma splices, dangling modifiers, agreement faults and faulty parallelism.
A participle phrase at the start of a sentence must describe the subject of the main clause.
A gerund is a verbal noun; an -ing word after a preposition is a gerund.
Enjoy, avoid, finish, suggest take the gerund; decide, hope, refuse, promise take the infinitive.
Items joined by and, or and but must have the same grammatical form.
